title: Operating Systems
html:
Operating Systems

Worth knowing because the abstractions leak. Latency, memory pressure and stalled threads are all operating-system behaviour surfacing in application code.

Process and thread

A process owns an address space. A thread is a unit of scheduling inside one, sharing that space with its siblings.

The consequences: processes are isolated, so a crash takes one down rather than all; threads share memory, which is why they are cheap to switch between and why they need synchronisation.

Context switching costs more than the register save implies - the cache is now full of the wrong data, and the TLB may be flushed. This is why a thread per request stops scaling and why async I/O exists: a thread waiting on the network is a thread not doing work while still consuming a stack.

Memory

Virtual memory gives each process a private address space, mapped to physical pages by the MMU. Consequences you can observe: a page fault is a disk read wearing the costume of a memory access; malloc succeeding does not mean the memory exists yet; and touching memory in a scattered order is slower than touching it in order, because prefetching cannot help.

The hierarchy is the number worth remembering. Registers and L1 are a cycle or two, main memory is a couple of hundred, an SSD is tens of thousands, and a network round trip is millions. Optimising anything without knowing which level you are on is guesswork.

Stack and heap. The stack is small, fast and automatically reclaimed; recursion too deep overflows it. The heap is large, slower to allocate, and must be reclaimed by you or a collector.

Concurrency

Race condition - the result depends on timing. Critical section - the code that must not interleave. Mutex - one holder at a time. Semaphore - up to n holders. Deadlock - a cycle of waiting, which needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption and circular wait all at once. Break any one and it cannot happen; the usual practical fix is a global lock ordering.

Atomicity is not the same as visibility. A value written by one thread may not be observed by another without a memory barrier, whatever the ordering of the source lines suggests.

The advice that follows from all this: prefer not sharing. Immutable data and message passing remove whole classes of these bugs rather than managing them.

I/O

Blocking - the thread waits. Non-blocking - it returns immediately and you check later. Asynchronous - you are notified on completion.

At scale the difference is decisive: a thread per connection costs a stack and a scheduling slot each, while an event loop over non-blocking sockets handles many thousands on a handful of threads.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming the memory order of your source is the order the hardware uses.
  • Blocking a thread-pool thread on I/O, starving the pool.
  • Adding threads to a CPU-bound workload beyond the core count, and paying only switching cost.
  • Treating a page fault or a cache miss as free.
  • Locking a large region because it is simpler, and serialising the whole system.
